sources.title: Preparing Your Older Child for a New Baby: How to Help Siblings Adjust
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (last updated 2/10/2026; adapted from Welcoming a New Sibling: How to Help Your Child Adjust, AAP 2020)
sources.quote: Expect your child to regress a little. For example, your toilet-trained child might suddenly start having "accidents," or they might want to take a bottle. This is normal and is your older child's way of making sure they still have your love and attention. Instead of telling them to act their age, let him have the attention they need. Praise them when they act more grown-up. Set aside special time for your child. ... Find ways to invite your child to help. ... Make an effort to spend some time alone with them each day. ... Read children's books about newborns and siblings with your child. ... Show your child their baby pictures. ... At this age, your child is still learning how to share with others and may feel like they need to compete for your attention.
sources.supports: After a new baby arrives an older child may regress (toilet accidents, wanting a bottle); AAP calls this normal and the child's way of making sure they still have the parents' love and attention. Advice: do not tell them to act their age, give the attention they need, praise grown-up behaviour, set aside special time alone each day, invite the child to help, read children's books about newborns and siblings. 'Show your child their baby pictures' and 'compete for your attention' are in the preschooler (2 to 4) section, listed before the baby arrives.

sources.title: Preparing Your Child for a New Sibling
sources.publisher: Child Mind Institute (writer Juliann Garey; clinical experts Mandi Silverman, PsyD, MBA, and Kristin Carothers, PhD; last reviewed or updated on January 2, 2026)
sources.quote: Regression behaviors like wanting bottles are normal ways for children to seek attention and will pass with time. ... establish a ritual (even if it’s just a few minutes of playtime or reading) that each parent can do with them before the arrival of the new baby and that continues after the new sibling comes. ... Even the best-prepared kids may suddenly start acting younger, and seeking the kind of attention their new sibling gets. For example, your toilet-trained child might start having accidents or want to go back to wearing diapers or they might want to take a bottle. “It is totally normal for children to engage in regressive behaviors when a new baby arrives,” Dr. Carothers says. “It’s children’s way of making sure their parents are aware that they still need them and it helps them to get the attention they crave. ... To help them feel valued, it can be good to give older children developmentally appropriate jobs that make them feel special. It’s also good to praise the positive mature behaviors the child exhibits. ... Another child may be the one that brings over the burp cloth or maybe they stand on a step stool and help with diaper changes or they can hold the towel at bath time. ... Board books and picture books about new babies are a great thing to add to the usual bedtime ritual.
sources.supports: Regression after a new baby (accidents, diapers, a bottle) is normal, is a way to seek the attention the baby gets, and passes with time. Advice: a small daily ritual with each parent, small jobs that make the older child feel special (bringing the burp cloth, helping with diaper changes, holding the towel at bath time), praise for mature behaviour, and picture books about new babies in the bedtime ritual (said for ages 2 to 4). Read in the in-app browser (the site blocks scripted fetching).

sources.title: Preparing Your Child for a New Sibling
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (reviewed by KidsHealth Medical Experts; no review date shown on the page)
sources.quote: It's common for them to feel jealousy toward the newborn and to act out. ... Take advantage of chances for one-on-one time with older kids. Spend time together while the baby is sleeping and, if possible, set aside time each day for older kids to get one parent's undivided attention. Knowing that there's special time just for them may help ease any resentment or anger about the new baby. ... Encourage older kids to talk about their feelings about the new baby. If a child cannot express those feelings, don't be surprised if they test limits or revert to speaking in baby talk. If your child acts up, don't bend the rules, but understand what feelings may be motivating that behavior. It could be a sign that your child needs more one-on-one time with you
sources.supports: Jealousy and acting out toward a newborn are common. Advice: one-on-one time while the baby sleeps, a set time each day with one parent's full attention, encouraging the older child to talk about feelings about the baby; a child who cannot express them may test limits or go back to baby talk.

sources.title: Preparing Your Older Child for a New Baby: How to Help Siblings Adjust
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (last updated 2/10/2026; adapted from Welcoming a New Sibling: How to Help Your Child Adjust, AAP 2020)
sources.quote: Expect your child to regress a little. For example, your toilet-trained child might suddenly start having "accidents," or they might want to take a bottle. This is normal and is your older child's way of making sure they still have your love and attention. Instead of telling them to act their age, let him have the attention they need. Praise them when they act more grown-up. Set aside special time for your child. ... Find ways to invite your child to help. ... Make an effort to spend some time alone with them each day. ... Read children's books about newborns and siblings with your child. ... Show your child their baby pictures. ... At this age, your child is still learning how to share with others and may feel like they need to compete for your attention.
sources.supports: After a new baby arrives an older child may regress (toilet accidents, wanting a bottle); AAP calls this normal and the child's way of making sure they still have the parents' love and attention. Advice: do not tell them to act their age, give the attention they need, praise grown-up behaviour, set aside special time alone each day, invite the child to help, read children's books about newborns and siblings. 'Show your child their baby pictures' and 'compete for your attention' are in the preschooler (2 to 4) section, listed before the baby arrives.

sources.title: Preparing Your Child for a New Sibling
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (reviewed by KidsHealth Medical Experts; no review date shown on the page)
sources.quote: It's common for them to feel jealousy toward the newborn and to act out. ... Take advantage of chances for one-on-one time with older kids. Spend time together while the baby is sleeping and, if possible, set aside time each day for older kids to get one parent's undivided attention. Knowing that there's special time just for them may help ease any resentment or anger about the new baby. ... Encourage older kids to talk about their feelings about the new baby. If a child cannot express those feelings, don't be surprised if they test limits or revert to speaking in baby talk. If your child acts up, don't bend the rules, but understand what feelings may be motivating that behavior. It could be a sign that your child needs more one-on-one time with you
sources.supports: Jealousy and acting out toward a newborn are common. Advice: one-on-one time while the baby sleeps, a set time each day with one parent's full attention, encouraging the older child to talk about feelings about the baby; a child who cannot express them may test limits or go back to baby talk.

sources.title: Preparing Your Child for a New Sibling
sources.publisher: Child Mind Institute (writer Juliann Garey; clinical experts Mandi Silverman, PsyD, MBA, and Kristin Carothers, PhD; last reviewed or updated on January 2, 2026)
sources.quote: Regression behaviors like wanting bottles are normal ways for children to seek attention and will pass with time. ... establish a ritual (even if it’s just a few minutes of playtime or reading) that each parent can do with them before the arrival of the new baby and that continues after the new sibling comes. ... Even the best-prepared kids may suddenly start acting younger, and seeking the kind of attention their new sibling gets. For example, your toilet-trained child might start having accidents or want to go back to wearing diapers or they might want to take a bottle. “It is totally normal for children to engage in regressive behaviors when a new baby arrives,” Dr. Carothers says. “It’s children’s way of making sure their parents are aware that they still need them and it helps them to get the attention they crave. ... To help them feel valued, it can be good to give older children developmentally appropriate jobs that make them feel special. It’s also good to praise the positive mature behaviors the child exhibits. ... Another child may be the one that brings over the burp cloth or maybe they stand on a step stool and help with diaper changes or they can hold the towel at bath time. ... Board books and picture books about new babies are a great thing to add to the usual bedtime ritual.
sources.supports: Regression after a new baby (accidents, diapers, a bottle) is normal, is a way to seek the attention the baby gets, and passes with time. Advice: a small daily ritual with each parent, small jobs that make the older child feel special (bringing the burp cloth, helping with diaper changes, holding the towel at bath time), praise for mature behaviour, and picture books about new babies in the bedtime ritual (said for ages 2 to 4). sources.quote: Expect your child to regress a little. For example, your toilet-trained child might suddenly start having "accidents," or they might want to take a bottle. Praise them when they act more grown-up. Set aside special time for your child. ... Find ways to invite your child to help. ... Make an effort to spend some time alone with them each day. ... Read children's books about newborns and siblings with your child. ... Show your child their baby pictures. ... At this age, your child is still learning how to share with others and may feel like they need to compete for your attention.

sources.publisher: Child Mind Institute (writer Juliann Garey; clinical experts Mandi Silverman, PsyD, MBA, and Kristin Carothers, PhD; last reviewed or updated on January 2, 2026)
sources.quote: Regression behaviors like wanting bottles are normal ways for children to seek attention and will pass with time. ... establish a ritual (even if it’s just a few minutes of playtime or reading) that each parent can do with them before the arrival of the new baby and that continues after the new sibling comes. ... To help them feel valued, it can be good to give older children developmentally appropriate jobs that make them feel special. sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (last updated 2/10/2026; adapted from Welcoming a New Sibling: How to Help Your Child Adjust, AAP 2020)
sources.quote: Expect your child to regress a little. For example, your toilet-trained child might suddenly start having "accidents," or they might want to take a bottle. This is normal and is your older child's way of making sure they still have your love and attention. Instead of telling them to act their age, let him have the attention they need. Praise them when they act more grown-up. Set aside special time for your child. ... Find ways to invite your child to help. ... Make an effort to spend some time alone with them each day. ... Read children's books about newborns and siblings with your child. ... Show your child their baby pictures. ... At this age, your child is still learning how to share with others and may feel like they need to compete for your attention.
sources.supports: After a new baby arrives an older child may regress (toilet accidents, wanting a bottle); AAP calls this normal and the child's way of making sure they still have the parents' love and attention. Advice: do not tell them to act their age, give the attention they need, praise grown-up behaviour, set aside special time alone each day, invite the child to help, read children's books about newborns and siblings. 'Show your child their baby pictures' and 'compete for your attention' are in the preschooler (2 to 4) section, listed before the baby arrives.

sources.title: Preparing Your Child for a New Sibling
sources.publisher: Child Mind Institute (writer Juliann Garey; clinical experts Mandi Silverman, PsyD, MBA, and Kristin Carothers, PhD; last reviewed or updated on January 2, 2026)
sources.quote: Regression behaviors like wanting bottles are normal ways for children to seek attention and will pass with time. ... establish a ritual (even if it’s just a few minutes of playtime or reading) that each parent can do with them before the arrival of the new baby and that continues after the new sibling comes. ... Even the best-prepared kids may suddenly start acting younger, and seeking the kind of attention their new sibling gets. For example, your toilet-trained child might start having accidents or want to go back to wearing diapers or they might want to take a bottle. “It is totally normal for children to engage in regressive behaviors when a new baby arrives,” Dr. Carothers says. “It’s children’s way of making sure their parents are aware that they still need them and it helps them to get the attention they crave. ... To help them feel valued, it can be good to give older children developmentally appropriate jobs that make them feel special. It’s also good to praise the positive mature behaviors the child exhibits. ... Another child may be the one that brings over the burp cloth or maybe they stand on a step stool and help with diaper changes or they can hold the towel at bath time. ... Board books and picture books about new babies are a great thing to add to the usual bedtime ritual.
sources.supports: Regression after a new baby (accidents, diapers, a bottle) is normal, is a way to seek the attention the baby gets, and passes with time. Advice: a small daily ritual with each parent, small jobs that make the older child feel special (bringing the burp cloth, helping with diaper changes, holding the towel at bath time), praise for mature behaviour, and picture books about new babies in the bedtime ritual (said for ages 2 to 4).
